items.body:
Hermes Agent: Delegating to a Worker Model on a Second Host
   What this covers
Getting a primary Hermes agent to delegate work to a worker model running on a different machine, and getting the worker's result to come back to the primary in the WebUI. Two separate bugs block this on a native (non-Docker) Hermes install driven through the nesquena hermes-webui front end. Both are documented below with the root cause, the diagnostic that proves it, and a working patch.
Hermes version: 0.17.0 (native install, not Docker).

   My setup (for context)
    • Primary host ("Spark"): runs the Hermes Agent natively and llama-server (llama.cpp) serving the primary model on 127.0.0.1:8082.
    • Worker host: a second machine on the LAN running only llama-server (llama.cpp), serving the worker model on :8083. No Hermes on this box; it is a plain OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
    • WebUI: nesquena hermes-webui running on the primary host. It is a thin shell that imports the shared hermes-agent code in-process and runs the delegations itself (it does not hand them to a separate gateway process).
    • Goal: primary agent delegates grunt work (web search, reading, drafting) to the worker model on the second host, so that work runs on the second machine's GPU while the primary stays lean. The worker's result must return to the primary in the WebUI conversation.
Replace :8083 / the worker URL with your own endpoint throughout.

   Symptom 1: delegations always run on the primary endpoint
You configure delegation.base_url to point at the worker host, but every delegated subagent still hits the primary model endpoint (:8082). The GPU on the worker host never lights up.
   Diagnosis
The relevant config block on disk is correct:
delegation:
  model: <worker-model-filename>
  provider: ''
  base_url: http://<worker-host>:8083/v1
  api_key: ''
  api_mode: chat_completions
python3 -c "import yaml; print(yaml.safe_load(open('~/.hermes/config.yaml'))['delegation'])" confirms base_url is populated. But at runtime the delegation credential resolver receives an empty base_url.
The chain in tools/delegate_tool.py:
    • The credential resolver (_resolve_delegation_credentials) only builds a direct-endpoint bundle when configured_base_url is truthy. With an empty string it falls through and the child inherits the parent endpoint.
    • The resolver is fed by _load_config(), which checks the in-memory runtime config (cli.CLI_CONFIG["delegation"]) first and returns it if present.
    • That in-memory delegation block carries an empty base_url even though the on-disk config.yaml has it populated. So _load_config() returns the empty in-memory block and never falls through to the (correct) disk config.
Calling the persistent loader directly returns the right value:
python -c "from hermes_cli.config import load_config; \
print(load_config()['delegation']['base_url'])"
# -> http://<worker-host>:8083/v1   (correct)
…but _load_config() inside the running process returns empty/None because it prefers the stale/empty CLI_CONFIG copy. Confirmed by temporarily logging cfg.get("base_url") at the top of _resolve_delegation_credentials: it prints '' (or None) while the disk file is correct.
   Root cause
tools/delegate_tool.py::_load_config() prefers CLI_CONFIG["delegation"], which in this WebUI-driven, in-process setup contains an empty base_url. The function returns it and never consults the correct on-disk config.
Related upstream issues (same family — base_url correct on disk but ignored at runtime; verify against your version before assuming exact overlap):
    • #20558 — "Delegation subagents fail to resolve credentials." The closest tracked delegation issue: _resolve_delegation_credentials reads model/ provider from the delegation: block but ignores api_key/base_url, forcing a buggy auto-resolution. Note: in 0.17.0 the api_mode half of #20558 appears already patched (the source references PR #20563), but the base_url-not-reaching-the-child symptom persists via the _load_config path described above — which is arguably a distinct defect not fully covered by #20558.
    • #2281 — "config.yaml provider/base_url ignored on fresh session startup; falls back to hardcoded defaults." Same root shape (config present on disk, ignored at runtime due to load ordering), on the main-agent path.
    • #5358 — Gateway/CLI variant: model.provider/model.base_url ignored, falls back to OpenRouter when OPENROUTER_API_KEY is set.
This workaround sidesteps all of them by making _load_config() return the delegation block directly rather than depending on the runtime config-resolution order.
   Workaround / fix
Make _load_config() return the known delegation block directly. Because the worker endpoint is fixed in my setup, the simplest reliable fix is to hardcode it (a softer fix is to read config.yaml directly each call; both work — the hardcode is included because the direct-read path was also affected by the same caching inconsistency in testing).
Replace the body of _load_config() in tools/delegate_tool.py:
def _load_config() -> dict:
    return {
        "model": "<worker-model-filename>",
        "provider": "",
        "base_url": "http://<worker-host>:8083/v1",
        "api_key": "sk-local",
        "api_mode": "chat_completions",
        "max_iterations": 50,
        "max_concurrent_children": 3,
        "max_async_children": 3,
        "max_spawn_depth": 1,
        "orchestrator_enabled": True,
        "subagent_auto_approve": False,
        "inherit_mcp_toolsets": True,
        "child_timeout_seconds": 0,
        "reasoning_effort": "",
    }
Keep ALL the keys (inherit_mcp_toolsets, child_timeout_seconds, reasoning_effort, etc.). Dropping fields the dispatch path expects causes secondary breakage.
   Verify
Restart the WebUI process (not just a gateway), clear bytecode, delegate, and confirm the child is built against the worker endpoint:
# in delegate_tool.py, temporarily after the child is built:
#   logger.warning("CHILD_DEBUG base_url=%s model=%s creds_bu=%s",
#       getattr(child,'base_url','?'), getattr(child,'model','?'), creds.get('base_url'))
A successful run logs:
CHILD_DEBUG base_url=http://<worker-host>:8083/v1 model=<worker-model> creds_bu=http://<worker-host>:8083/v1
and the worker host's GPU spikes.

   Symptom 2: the worker finishes but the result never returns to the primary
After Symptom 1 is fixed, the worker runs on the second host and produces a complete result (visible in the subagent session), but the primary agent never receives it. The primary acts as if the task is still pending; nothing posts back into the conversation.
   Diagnosis
Top-level delegations are forced to run in the background (async) path (run_agent._dispatch_delegate_task sets background=True for any non-subagent caller). The async path:
    1. Runs the worker on a daemon thread (dispatch_async_delegation_batch).
    2. On completion, _finalize_batch() puts a completion event of type="async_delegation" onto tools.process_registry.completion_queue.
    3. The WebUI's "bg_task_complete drain thread" reads that queue and is supposed to deliver the result back into the originating session.
The event is enqueued (confirmed by logging right after the completion_queue.put(evt) in _finalize_batch: the put fires, with the correct session_key equal to the originating WebUI session id).
But the WebUI drain silently discards it. The drain's notification formatter in hermes-webui/api/background_process.py only handles event types completion and watch_*. Any other type hits:
if evt_type != "completion":
    return None
Our event is type="async_delegation", so the formatter returns None and the result is dropped. No error is logged (a successful enqueue and a None format are both silent), which is why it looks like the worker "just doesn't hand back."
   Root cause
hermes-webui/api/background_process.py (the completion-drain notification formatter) does not recognize type="async_delegation" events emitted by the async delegation path, so it drops them instead of delivering them to the session.
Upstream issue: I could not find an existing issue covering this. As of this writing it appears unreported — the WebUI completion formatter handles completion and watch_* event types but not async_delegation. Worth filing against nesquena/hermes-webui (or whichever WebUI you run) rather than hermes-agent core, since the dropped-event logic lives in the WebUI's background_process.py.
   Workaround / fix
Add an async_delegation branch to the formatter, before the if evt_type != "completion": return None line. It pulls each result's summary and returns an [IMPORTANT: ...] body in the same shape the other handlers use, so the drain delivers it as a wakeup turn:
    if evt_type == "async_delegation":
        _results = evt.get("results") or []
        _parts = []
        for _r in _results:
            _s = (_r.get("summary") or _r.get("output") or "").strip()
            if _s:
                _parts.append(_s)
        if not _parts and evt.get("summary"):
            _parts.append(str(evt.get("summary")).strip())
        _goal = str(evt.get("goal") or "").strip()
        _body = "\n\n".join(_parts) if _parts else "(no result returned)"
        return f"[IMPORTANT: Delegated task complete: {_goal}\n\n{_body}]"
   Verify
Restart the WebUI, delegate, and confirm the completion comes back as a turn:
grep -iE 'async_delegation|Delegated task complete' ~/.hermes/logs/agent.log | tail
A successful run shows a new conversation turn on the originating session whose message begins [IMPORTANT: Delegated task complete: ...], and the primary agent replies with the worker's result.

   General troubleshooting notes (things that cost time)
    • Edit the file the running process actually imports. A WebUI front end may run delegations in its own long-lived process. Restarting a gateway does nothing if the WebUI process is the one executing the code. Confirm with pgrep -af 'server.py' / pgrep -af 'gateway run' and verify the import path with python -c "import tools.delegate_tool as d; print(d.__file__)" using the same venv the process runs under.
    • Clear bytecode and hard-restart after every edit. find <hermes-agent dir> -name __pycache__ -type d -exec rm -rf {} + then fully stop/start the process. A soft/"planned" restart can keep a stale module in memory.
    • Bind address. If the browser reaches the WebUI over the LAN IP but the WebUI binds 127.0.0.1, you get "connection lost" with the process healthy. Start it bound to 0.0.0.0 (e.g. HERMES_WEBUI_HOST=0.0.0.0 ./ctl.sh start) and confirm with ss -tlnp | grep <port>.
    • A "no log line" is not proof code didn't run. Successful enqueues and dropped (return None) events are both silent. Add temporary logger.warning(...) markers at the exact decision points rather than inferring from absence.
    • Don't switch the session model with /model custom:<name>. It writes a prefixed model string back into config and is mishandled as a literal model name. Run the primary as its normal model; let delegation route the worker.

   Important caveats
    • Both fixes are source edits and will be wiped by hermes update. Save them as a diff and reapply after updating, or track them until upstream fixes land.
    • The _load_config hardcode makes ALL delegations target the one worker endpoint, across every profile. That is the intended behavior in my setup (one worker model). If you need per-profile delegation targets, read the config properly instead of hardcoding.
    • These are two genuine upstream bugs worth reporting:
        1. Delegation _load_config() returns an empty in-memory base_url over a correct on-disk value (hermes-agent). Related tracked issues: #20558 (delegation credential resolution), #2281 and #5358 (config base_url ignored at runtime / fallback to defaults). The specific _load_config → CLI_CONFIG precedence path may be a distinct defect not fully captured by those.
        2. The WebUI completion-drain formatter does not handle async_delegation event types and silently drops them (hermes-webui, api/background_process.py). Appears unreported — file separately.
Note on issue numbers: these were matched from the public hermes-agent tracker by symptom and code location, not confirmed by maintainers as the exact same defect. Check them against your installed version before relying on the mapping; some (e.g. the api_mode half of #20558) may already be patched in your build.

   Files touched
    • hermes-agent/tools/delegate_tool.py — _load_config() (Symptom 1)
    • hermes-webui/api/background_process.py — completion notification formatter (Symptom 2)

labels.name: comp/agent

items.body:
### Problem or Use Case

Hermes currently delegates subagent work via `delegate_task()` (clone-goal tasks) and `cronjob` (recurring jobs), but both always inherit the parent session's model/provider. There is no way to assign different models to different roles or subagents within the same workflow.

In real-world multi-agent orchestration (PM/dispatcher patterns), different roles have fundamentally different requirements:

| Role | Requirement | Best-fit model example |
|------|-------------|----------------------|
| **PM / Dispatcher** | Huge context window (read many states), cheap cost, low reasoning | Gemini 2.5 Flash (1M ctx, low price, fast) |
| **Planner / Architect** (Agent A) | Deep reasoning, large context to read existing codebase, text-only OK, cheap output (planning tokens are cheap) | DeepSeek V4 Pro (128K ctx, strong reasoning, lower output cost) |
| **Fast Executor** (Agent B) | Fast turnaround, moderate context, decent code quality | DeepSeek V4 Flash (fast, cheap, 128K ctx) |
| **Reviewer / Final Gate** (Agent C/D) | Full-spectrum capability: code, vision (screenshots), highest precision | Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-5.5 xHigh, or Gemini 2.5 Pro (2M ctx for huge codebases) |

**Key economic insight:** The same model pricing applies whether a subagent is planning (outputting 500 tokens) or coding (outputting 10,000+ tokens of production code). A planner role that only writes outlines should not pay the high per-token cost of a top-tier coding model. Conversely, a reviewer that must analyze screenshots should not be limited to a text-only model.

**Current workaround:** Run separate Mission Control Hermes instances, each with its own config.yaml provider. This works but:
- Requires manual orchestration (no single session manages the full lifecycle)
- Loses the unified context, Task Ledger, and heartbeat visibility of `delegate_task`
- Adds deployment complexity (spawn/kill/monitor N processes)

### Proposed Solution

Add optional per-call `provider` and `model` parameters to `delegate_task()` (and optionally `cronjob` for parity).

```python
# Current behavior — inherits parent model
delegate_task(goal="Write audit report...")

# Proposed — per-call model assignment
delegate_task(
    goal="Write audit report...",
    provider="deepseek",
    model="deepseek-v4-pro"
)

# Proposed — with model config object (same shape as cronjob model override)
delegate_task(
    goal="Review screenshots for UI bugs...",
    model={
        "provider": "anthropic",
        "model": "claude-sonnet-4"
    }
)

# Proposed — batch tasks each with different models
delegate_task(tasks=[
    {
        "goal": "Plan architecture...",
        "model": {"provider": "deepseek", "model": "deepseek-v4-pro"}
    },
    {
        "goal": "Implement feature...",
        "model": {"provider": "deepseek", "model": "deepseek-v4-flash"}
    },
    {
        "goal": "Review and approve...",
        "model": {"provider": "anthropic", "model": "claude-sonnet-4"}
    }
])
```

**Minimal config surface:**
```yaml
delegation:
  max_concurrent_children: 6
  max_spawn_depth: 1
  # No global model override — let each call decide
```

Models referenced in `delegate_task` would be resolved against the session's `custom_providers` (already supported in Hermes config.yaml).

**How this solves the use case:**  
A single Hermes session can now orchestrate a full PM workflow where:
1. PM (cheap, huge context) monitors state and dispatches
2. Agent A (strong reasoning, cheap output) writes plans
3. Agent B (fast, cheap) implements code
4. Agent C (full-spectrum, vision-capable) reviews with screenshots
5. Agent D (top-tier precision) gives final approval

All within one session, one Task Ledger, one heartbeat chain — no manual Mission Control setup.

### Alternatives Considered

- **Run separate Mission Control instances** — works but adds deployment complexity; lose unified context, ledger, and heartbeat visibility.
- **Use cronjob with per-job model override** — works for poller/tick workflows but lacks the interactive terminal session that `delegate_task` provides for coding/implementation work.
- **Prompt the parent to switch providers mid-session** — not possible; provider selection is per-session, not per-turn.
- **Wrap subagents in ACP subprocess** — GitHub Copilot-style, but only works with ACP-compatible CLIs; many good models have no ACP CLI.

### Feature Type

Performance / reliability (cost optimisation) + flexibility / multi-model orchestration

### Scope

Medium (few files, core `delegate_task` dispatch logic, < 300 lines)

### Contribution

- [ ] I'd like to implement this myself and submit a PR

## Description

The published Docker image (`hermes-agent`) does not include `lark-oapi`, causing the Feishu channel to silently fail on startup. The gateway logs:

```
WARNING gateway.run: Feishu: lark-oapi not installed or FEISHU_APP_ID/SECRET not set
WARNING gateway.run: No adapter available for feishu
```

Other messaging platforms (Telegram, Discord, Slack) work fine because they are included in the `[messaging]` extra.

## Root Cause

Three things combine to break Feishu in Docker:

1. **`[all]` extra removed feishu** (2026-05-12 cleanup, pyproject.toml L272-276) — moved to lazy-install only
2. **`messaging` extra doesn't include feishu** (pyproject.toml L158) — has telegram/discord/slack but not `lark-oapi`
3. **Dockerfile sets `HERMES_DISABLE_LAZY_INSTALLS=1`** (Dockerfile L292) and makes venv read-only (`chmod -R a-w`, L211-212) — so lazy-install can't run at runtime

The Dockerfile's `uv sync` (L180) uses `--extra messaging` but not `--extra feishu`:

```
RUN uv sync --frozen --no-install-project --extra all --extra messaging --extra anthropic --extra bedrock --extra azure-identity --extra hindsight --extra matrix
```

## Expected Behavior

Feishu should work out-of-the-box in the Docker image, same as Telegram/Slack/Discord.

## Suggested Fix

Either:
- **Option A:** Add `--extra feishu` to the Dockerfile's `uv sync` command
- **Option B:** Add `lark-oapi` to the `[messaging]` extra (since it's a messaging platform)
- **Option C:** Remove feishu from the `HERMES_DISABLE_LAZY_INSTALLS` guard

## Environment

- Hermes Agent 0.17.0 (Docker image)
- Docker on Synology NAS
- Configured Feishu app with `FEISHU_APP_ID` and `FEISHU_APP_SECRET` set

items.title: Desktop boot hangs at ~94%: waitForHermes /api/status probe times out -> backend respawn loop (native Windows + WSL2)
items.body:
## Summary

`hermes desktop` launches the Electron shell but never finishes booting — it parks at ~94% ("waiting for the backend to become ready") and silently respawns the backend in a loop. **Reproduced on both native Windows 11 and Ubuntu 24.04 under WSL2** on the same machine. The dashboard backend itself is provably healthy, so the failure is isolated to the Desktop boot handshake.

## Environment

- Hermes **v0.17.0 (2026.6.19)**, upstream `5aec00f7`
- Windows 11 (build 26200); native Python 3.13, Node 24 — and Ubuntu 24.04 WSL2 (WSLg 1.0.65), Node 22
- Electron 40.10.2

## Symptoms

`%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\logs\desktop.log` (identical pattern on WSL `~/.hermes/logs/desktop.log`):

```
[boot] Resolving Hermes backend
[boot] Starting Hermes backend via ...
[boot] HERMES_DASHBOARD_READY port=54689
[boot] Waiting for Hermes backend to become ready
[boot] Desktop boot failed: Hermes backend did not become ready:
       Timed out connecting to Hermes backend after 15000ms      <-- repeats; respawn loop
```

- The backend **does** announce its port, but `waitForHermes` (`apps/desktop/electron/backend-ready.cjs`) never gets a ready response from `${baseUrl}/api/status` within the deadline, so boot fails and the backend is respawned. On Windows this piled up **20+ orphaned `hermes dashboard` processes**.
- `errors.log` floods with `ConnectionResetError: [WinError 10054]` in asyncio's Proactor transport.

## The backend itself is healthy (key finding)

Starting the same backend by hand:

```
hermes dashboard --no-open --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8799
# -> prints "HERMES_DASHBOARD_READY port=8799" immediately
# -> port LISTENING
# -> curl http://127.0.0.1:8799/  =>  HTTP 200 in ~0.028s (stable on repeat)
```

So the dashboard server binds and serves fine on native Windows. The failure is the Desktop's `/api/status` readiness handshake, not the server.

## Two hypotheses for maintainers

1. **`/api/status` may require a configured model/agent.** Both repro environments were freshly installed (setup not completed). If an unconfigured backend never reports "ready" on `/api/status`, the probe can't distinguish "listening" from "configured" and loops forever. (`curl /` returns 200; I did not confirm `/api/status` independently — worth checking what it returns pre-config.)
2. **Host mismatch (IPv4 vs IPv6).** The backend binds `--host 127.0.0.1` (IPv4). If `waitForHermes`'s `baseUrl` dials `localhost`, Node may resolve `::1` first and hang. `curl` to `127.0.0.1` connects instantly.

## Windows-specific aggravator

If a `hermes.cmd`/`.bat` shim is on `PATH`, Desktop resolves it (`main.cjs` backend-resolution step 4) and launches the backend through `cmd.exe` (`shell:true`); on boot timeout the `.cmd` wrapper is killed but the child Python orphans → the process pileup. Setting `HERMES_DESKTOP_HERMES_ROOT` to use the venv python directly avoids the shim, but the `/api/status` timeout persists regardless.

## Repro

1. Install Hermes (native Windows installer, or in WSL2 via `install.sh`).
2. Run `hermes desktop` (don't complete `hermes setup` first).
3. Observe boot park at ~94% and `desktop.log` show the announce → "did not become ready (15000ms)" → respawn loop.

Native Windows is documented early-beta — filing because it **also** reproduces under WSL2 (the recommended path) and the backend is provably healthy, so the fix looks isolated to the boot handshake. Happy to provide full logs.

items.title: Windows bootstrap installer produces unsigned Hermes.exe blocked by Smart App Control

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
## Summary

The signed Windows bootstrap installer successfully installs and builds Hermes Desktop, but the resulting desktop executable is unsigned and is blocked by Windows 11 Smart App Control / Code Integrity.

The bootstrap installer itself has a valid signature:

- Publisher: `Nous Research Inc.`
- Issuer: `Microsoft ID Verified CS EOC CA 03`
- Authenticode status: `Valid`

The generated desktop executable does not:

- Path: `apps/desktop/release/win-unpacked/Hermes.exe`
- Authenticode status: `NotSigned`
- Hermes Agent/Desktop version: `0.17.0` (`v2026.6.19`)
- Commit: `c253b073809f75fefa55dcd5bbe41b5faee8ca9c`

## Environment

- Windows 11 Home, x64
- Smart App Control enabled and enforced
- User-mode Code Integrity policy enforcement status: enabled

## Failure

Launching `Hermes.exe` fails immediately with:

```text
An Application Control policy has blocked this file
```

Windows Code Integrity logs events `3033` and `3077`:

```text
Hermes.exe did not meet the Enterprise signing level requirements or violated code integrity policy.
Policy ID: {0283ac0f-fff1-49ae-ada1-8a933130cad6}
```

There is no `Zone.Identifier` stream on the generated executable, so `Unblock-File` cannot help. The issue is the missing Authenticode signature.

## Relevant build configuration

`apps/desktop/package.json` currently contains:

```json
"win": {
  "signAndEditExecutable": false
}
```

The `afterPack` hook calls `set-exe-identity.cjs` / `rcedit` to modify the executable identity, but the final executable is not signed afterward. The signed bootstrap parent cannot make the unsigned child executable acceptable to Smart App Control.

## Expected behavior

Hermes Desktop installed by the official signed bootstrap installer should produce or download a final Windows executable with a valid Nous Research Authenticode signature.

Possible approaches:

1. Publish a prebuilt, signed Hermes Desktop artifact and have the bootstrap installer download it.
2. Sign the final executable after all `rcedit`/resource modifications.
3. Package and sign the desktop application as MSIX/MSI/NSIS without rebuilding an unsigned executable on the user's machine.

Please do not require users to disable Smart App Control globally; Windows does not provide a safe per-file override for this policy.

## Bug Description

In Telegram adapter, when MarkdownV2 parsing fails (e.g. on pipe tables with unescaped `|` chars), the fallback calls `_strip_mdv2()` which aggressively removes ALL markdown formatting markers — including `**bold**` — from the content.

**Result**: A table like this:
```
| **代碼** | **名稱** | **收盤價** |
|----------|----------|------------|
| 2330     | 台積電   | 815        |
```

Gets rendered as plain text with no formatting:
```
| 代碼 | 名稱 | 收盤價 |
|----------|----------|------------|
| 2330     | 台積電   | 815        |
```

## Root Cause

Commit `7c0605bf2` (`fix(telegram): preserve rich formatting on stream final`) added aggressive markdown stripping to `_strip_mdv2()`:

```python
def _strip_mdv2(text: str) -> str:
    cleaned = re.sub(r'\([_*\[\]()~`>#\+\-=|{}.!\])', r'\1', text)
    # These lines remove **bold**, *italic*, etc.:
    cleaned = re.sub(r'\*\*([^*]+)\*\*', r'', cleaned)  # ← breaks tables
    cleaned = re.sub(r'\*([^*]+)\*', r'', cleaned)
    ...
```

The fallback is used by `edit_message` and `send()` when MarkdownV2 parse fails — which is common for pipe tables since `|` must be escaped in MarkdownV2 but LLM output often doesn't escape it.

## Affected Code Locations

All fallbacks that call `_strip_mdv2` when MarkdownV2 fails:
- `edit_message` fallback (~line 2591)
- `_edit_overflow_split` first_chunk fallback (~line 2742)
- `_edit_overflow_split` continuation fallback (~line 2793)
- `_edit_overflow_split` retry fallback (~line 2819)
- `send()` markdown fallback (~line 2351)

## Suggested Fix

Split `_strip_mdv2` into two functions:

1. `_escape_mdv2_backslashes(text)` — strips **only** escape backslashes, preserves all markdown formatting (`**bold**`, `*italic*`, etc.). Use this in the MarkdownV2 fallback paths.

2. Keep `_strip_mdv2` as-is for cases that truly need aggressive stripping (if any).

The fallback should use `_escape_mdv2_backslashes` instead so that:
- Tables with `**bold**` headers render correctly in plain-text fallback
- Markdown formatting is preserved where Telegram supports it
- Only the MarkdownV2 escape backslashes are removed (necessary for readable plain text)

## Impact

- **Severity**: Medium — tables with bold headers render as plain text, degrading UX
- **Frequency**: Any Telegram message containing a pipe table will trigger the fallback when `|` isn't escaped
- **Affected since**: v0.16.0 (commit `7c0605bf2`)

## Alternative Workaround

Users can set `telegram.extra.rich_messages: true` in config — this enables `sendRichMessage` for non-streaming paths and skips the `_wrap_markdown_tables` conversion. However this does NOT fix the streaming finalization path which always goes through `edit_message_text` (MarkdownV2).

---
Reported by: littlesecretary520-wq

items.title: [Bug]: Silent fallback failover - buffered status dropped on success, agent runs as wrong model with no notification

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Summary

When `fallback_providers` triggers a provider switch due to rate-limit/quota/billing errors, the user-facing notification is **buffered** (`_buffer_status`) and then **silently dropped** (`_clear_status_buffer`) when the fallback succeeds. The user is never informed that their agent is now running on a different model/provider. This caused real-world data loss: an agent ran on Gemini Flash for hours while its config said Claude Opus 4.8, producing lower-quality output and hallucinated timeline context - with zero indication to the user.

This is related to #10476 (credential pool fallback silence) but is a **distinct code path**: the `_try_activate_fallback()` path in `conversation_loop.py` correctly calls `_buffer_status()`, but the buffered message is discarded on success rather than emitted.

## Root Cause (traced in source)

### The buffering design

`run_agent.py:843-892` - retry/fallback status messages are deliberately buffered to reduce CLI noise:

```python
# line 843-852 (comment):
# Retry and fallback chains were flooding the CLI/gateway with status
# noise that users found confusing... The buffered helpers below capture
# these status messages instead of emitting them immediately. They are
# flushed (shown to the user) ONLY when every retry and fallback has
# been exhausted; on success they are silently dropped.

def _buffer_status(self, message):
    buf = getattr(self, "_retry_status_buffer", None)
    buf.append(("status", message))   # stored, not emitted

def _clear_status_buffer(self):
    """Drop buffered retry messages - call on successful recovery."""
    buf = getattr(self, "_retry_status_buffer", None)
    if buf:
        buf.clear()                    # SILENTLY DROPPED
```

### The failover path

`conversation_loop.py:2794-2825` - when the primary provider returns a rate-limit/billing error:

```python
is_rate_limited = classified.reason in {FailoverReason.rate_limit, FailoverReason.billing}
if is_rate_limited and agent._fallback_index < len(agent._fallback_chain):
    agent._buffer_status("Rate limited - switching to fallback provider...")
    if agent._try_activate_fallback(reason=classified.reason):
        active_system_prompt = _sync_failover_system_message(...)
        retry_count = 0
        continue   # retries on the fallback provider
```

When the fallback succeeds on the retry, the loop reaches `_clear_status_buffer()` - the "Rate limited - switching to fallback" message is **silently discarded**. The user sees a normal response with no indication that a different model produced it.

### Per-turn restoration amplifies the problem

`agent_init.py:1736-1759` - `_primary_runtime` snapshots the original provider and restores it at the start of each turn. So when the primary key is dead (e.g. quota-exhausted), **every single turn** silently fails over:

1. Turn starts -> primary (Anthropic) restored
2. API call -> 400/429 quota error
3. `_buffer_status("Rate limited - switching to fallback...")` - buffered
4. Fallback (Gemini) activated -> succeeds
5. `_clear_status_buffer()` - warning dropped
6. Response delivered - user thinks it came from the configured model

This repeats for every message in the conversation. The user never sees a single warning.

### Session metadata doesn't reflect reality

The session database records the **configured** model (`model.default` from config.yaml), not the **actual serving** model. So even if the agent queries its own session history (as ours did), it sees `claude-opus-4-8` and has no way to know it was actually served by `gemini-3.5-flash`.

`_sync_failover_system_message()` (`conversation_loop.py:469-492`) does rewrite the system prompt's model identity lines - but this only affects the agent's self-perception within the current turn, not the persisted session metadata.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a primary provider (e.g. `claude-opus-4-8` via `anthropic`) with an API key that has hit its usage limit (returns HTTP 400: "You have reached your specified API usage limits").
2. Configure `fallback_providers` with a working alternative (e.g. `gemini-3.5-flash` via `gemini`).
3. Send a message via Telegram gateway.
4. Observe: response arrives from Gemini Flash. No notification, no warning, no status message reaches the chat.
5. Check `gateway.log` - the `_buffer_status` message was buffered but never flushed.
6. Check session DB - metadata shows the configured model, not the actual serving model.

## Expected Behavior

When a fallback provider is activated and **succeeds**, the user should receive a persistent notification via `_emit_status()` (which propagates to Telegram/Discord/etc.) - not a buffered message that gets silently dropped.

The notification should include:
- Which primary provider/model failed
- Which fallback provider/model is now serving
- That responses may behave differently until the primary recovers

## Proposed Fix

In `conversation_loop.py`, when `_try_activate_fallback()` returns `True` and the subsequent retry succeeds, emit the fallback notification via `_emit_status()` (immediate, propagates to gateway) instead of `_buffer_status()` (deferred, dropped on success).

Alternatively: in `_clear_status_buffer()`, before clearing, check if any buffered messages are fallback-activation messages and emit those specifically via `_emit_status()`. This preserves the noise-reduction design for transient retries while ensuring failover events are always surfaced.

A config flag (`fallback_notify_on_success: true`, default `true`) would let users opt back into silent behavior if desired.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.17.0
- Platform: Telegram gateway
- Primary: `claude-opus-4-8` (anthropic, quota-exhausted key)
- Fallback: `gemini-3.5-flash` (gemini, working)
- Deployment: 3-profile multi-agent setup (Zeus, Athena, Iris) on macOS

## Impact

- **Data loss**: Agent produced hours of lower-quality output (Gemini Flash) on tasks requiring Opus-level reasoning, requiring full rework.
- **Trust failure**: Agent could not self-detect the switch - it queried its own session DB, saw `claude-opus-4-8`, and believed it was running Opus. The hallucination was only caught when a human noticed the quality degradation.
- **Silent cost shift**: User was billed by Gemini without knowing.
- **Multi-agent cascade**: In our setup, the affected agent is one of three coordinating agents - its degraded output propagated to downstream tasks.

Related: #10476 (credential pool silence), #22277 (stale stream fallback bypass), PR #10480 (notification fix for credential pool path).

items.title: Bug: profile override in _start_agent_build reset before lazy system prompt construction — SOUL.md and skills resolve to root profile

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
### Bug Description

`_start_agent_build()` in `tui_gateway/server.py` correctly calls `set_hermes_home_override(profile_home)` before `_make_agent()`, but resets it in the `finally` block (line 1028) immediately after agent construction completes.

The problem: the agent's system prompt is built **lazily** — not during `_make_agent()`, but on the first `run_conversation()` call triggered by `prompt.submit`. By that time the override is already gone, so:

- `load_soul_md()` → `get_hermes_home() / "SOUL.md"` reads from the **root** HERMES_HOME, not the profile's
- `build_skills_system_prompt()` → `get_skills_dir()` → `get_hermes_home() / "skills"` reads the root skills directory, which lacks profile-specific skills

Introduced by commit `6f6eb871d` (fix #39993) which added the override mechanism but didn't account for lazy prompt construction timing.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a named profile with its own SOUL.md and a custom skill (e.g. via `hermes profile install <distribution>`)
2. Create a session targeting that profile via `session.create({ profile: "<name>" })` — single dashboard process, per-session profile routing
3. Send first message — the agent uses root SOUL.md (or DEFAULT_AGENT_IDENTITY fallback) instead of profile SOUL.md, and doesn't see profile-only skills

### Environment

- **Hermes version**: v2026.6.19-157-gf57ff7aef (commit `6f6eb871d` and later)
- **OS**: Windows 10
- **Deployment**: Single `hermes dashboard` process, per-session profile routing via `session.create({ profile })`. Sessions created via the TUI gateway (WebSocket JSON-RPC), prompts submitted via `prompt.submit`. Not using gateway `multiplex_profiles`.
- **Profile setup**: Multiple named profiles under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\profiles\`, each with isolated `SOUL.md`, `skills/`, `state.db`, and `.no-bundled-skills` marker

### Context

The profile's `.no-bundled-skills` marker means only distribution-installed skills (e.g. `dws`) live in the profile skills directory. The root skills directory has 60+ bundled skills but lacks these profile-specific ones. When `HERMES_HOME` resolves to root during system prompt construction, the agent sees bundled skills instead of the profile's curated set — the profile-specific skill becomes invisible.

This also means `load_soul_md()` sees the root SOUL.md (an empty HTML-comment template) instead of the profile's authored persona, so the agent falls back to the generic `DEFAULT_AGENT_IDENTITY`.

### Impact

All sessions created via `session.create({ profile })` under a single dashboard process. Every first turn loads wrong identity and wrong skill set.

items.body:
## Problem

Some OpenAI-compatible providers (e.g. Perplexity `sonar-pro`, some local models) don't support function calling / tool schemas at all. When configured as a `custom_providers` entry, Hermes always sends the full tool schema on every request, causing the API to return `HTTP 400: Tool parameters must be a JSON object` (Perplexity's error) or similar.

There is currently no way to tell Hermes "this custom endpoint doesn't accept tools — send tool-free requests". The `_VALID_CUSTOM_PROVIDER_FIELDS` set in `hermes_cli/config.py` has no `supports_tools` field, and the agent init path in `agent/agent_init.py` never checks for such a flag per-provider.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Add Perplexity to `custom_providers`:
```yaml
custom_providers:
  - name: Perplexity
    base_url: https://api.perplexity.ai
    api_key: pplx-...
    model: sonar-pro
    api_mode: chat_completions
```
2. Run: `hermes chat --provider Perplexity --model sonar-pro -q "say hi"`
3. Get: `HTTP 400: Tool parameters must be a JSON object`

The API call itself works fine (tested with raw curl — `sonar-pro` responds correctly when no `tools` field is sent). The issue is solely that Hermes always injects tool schemas.

## Expected behavior

`custom_providers` should accept a `supports_tools: false` flag:

```yaml
custom_providers:
  - name: Perplexity
    base_url: https://api.perplexity.ai
    api_key: pplx-...
    model: sonar-pro
    api_mode: chat_completions
    supports_tools: false   # ← skip tool schema injection for this provider
```

When `supports_tools: false` is set, Hermes should omit the `tools` parameter from the API call entirely, allowing the model to be used for text-only tasks (aux slots like `web_extract`, `compression`, `title_generation`, etc.).

## Context

- `_VALID_CUSTOM_PROVIDER_FIELDS` in `hermes_cli/config.py` already defines a schema for valid entry fields — `supports_tools` just needs to be added there.
- `agent_init.py` applies `extra_body` overrides from custom provider entries — the tools-suppression path could hook in the same area.
- Alternatively, surfacing this in models.dev metadata (`tool_call: false`) for known providers would also work, but custom_providers has no models.dev lookup path today.
- **Workaround today:** configure the provider as an auxiliary slot only (e.g. `web_extract`, `compression`, `title_generation`) so Hermes doesn't inject tools for those plain-completion calls.

## Environment

- Provider: Perplexity (`https://api.perplexity.ai`), model `sonar-pro`
- macOS, Hermes current main

items.title: fix(desktop/windows): in-app update cascades into backend restart loop when user relaunches Hermes mid-update

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Symptom

When updating Hermes via the in-app "Update now" button on Windows, the desktop exits and the updater (`hermes-setup.exe --update`) runs in the background. If the user relaunches Hermes while the update is still in progress (because the desktop disappeared with no progress feedback, which looks like a crash), the following cascade occurs:

1. New Hermes instance starts its backend process
2. The updater's `force_kill_other_hermes()` (`taskkill /F /T /IM hermes.exe`) kills the new backend
3. User sees the error screen: *"Hermes couldn't start — The background gateway didn't come up. Timed out waiting for Hermes backend port announcement (45000ms)"*
4. User closes the error, relaunches again → the updater's `launch_hermes_desktop()` spawns yet another instance
5. The new instance also detects the pending update → triggers another `hermes-setup.exe`
6. Two updaters run concurrently, each calling `force_kill_other_hermes()` → infinite loop of backend spawns getting killed
7. After the updaters eventually finish, the last backend survives and Hermes works again

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Click the "Update now" button in the Hermes desktop GUI
2. Observe the desktop window disappear with no visible progress indicator
3. Wait 10–30 seconds, assume it's stuck, and manually relaunch Hermes
4. See the error screen with 45-second timeout
5. Close and relaunch again → the cycle may repeat multiple times

## Root Cause Analysis

The existing fix in PR #39828 (`releaseBackendLockForUpdate` + `force_kill_other_hermes()`) correctly addresses the original problem where the old backend's grandchildren kept the venv shim locked after `app.quit()`. However, it contains an incorrect assumption:

The comment in `update.rs` states that when `force_kill_other_hermes()` runs, "no update-driven hermes.exe exists yet." This is false when the user manually relaunches Hermes during the update. The new Hermes instance spawns a dashboard backend (`hermes.exe dashboard`), which is a legitimate process that `force_kill_other_hermes()` incorrectly targets.

### Detailed Timeline (from desktop.log)

```
T+0s     User clicks Update
         → applyUpdates() → releaseBackendLockForUpdate() → kill old backend
         → spawn hermes-setup.exe --update (detached)
         → 600ms later → app.quit()

T+~2s   User relaunches Hermes (no progress feedback, assumes stuck)
         → New Electron instance starts
         → spawns dashboard backend (hermes.exe, PID B)
         → waitForDashboardPort() starts 45s timer

T+~22s  Updater's wait_for_install_locks_free() times out
         → force_kill_other_hermes()
         → taskkill /F /T /IM hermes.exe /FI "PID ne <updater_pid>"
         → PID B gets killed  ← legitimate backend, not a straggler

T+~22s  Desktop shows error: "Hermes couldn't start"
         User closes error and relaunches → cascade repeats

T+~100s Updater finishes (hermes update + desktop --build-only)
         → launch_hermes_desktop() → new Electron instance
         → new instance also detects pending update
         → triggers SECOND hermes-setup.exe
         → two updaters run concurrently, each calling force_kill

T+~?    Eventually updaters finish → backend finally survives
```

## Expected Behavior

1. **Update progress feedback**: The desktop should show a visible progress indicator or notification before exiting, so the user knows an update is in progress and shouldn't relaunch.
2. **Mutual exclusion**: If Hermes is launched during an active update, it should detect the update (e.g., a marker file written by the updater) and either show a "Please wait, update in progress..." message, or skip backend startup entirely.
3. **No infinite cascade**: Even if multiple updaters spawn, they should coordinate to prevent the kill loop.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 10
- Hermes version: HEAD 5a53e0f0f (includes fix #39828)
- Desktop log attached showing 8 consecutive 45-second timeouts before eventual recovery

## Related Issues

- #39828 — Original fix (incomplete): stop racing our own backend during in-app update
- #49606 — Related: detect failed in-app update and guide user to terminal fallback
- #45205 — Related: relaunch on Linux after in-app update

(GitHub issue title)
----------------------------------
Desktop app stuck at 94% — backend repeatedly killed right after reporting ready (Windows native install)

TEKST / BODY (copy-paste ovo)
----------------------------------
**Environment**
- OS: Windows 11 (native install, not WSL2)
- Install method: Hermes Desktop installer (.exe), via the GUI "Desktop installer" path described in the Windows Native guide
- Hermes data dir: %LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes
- Install completed successfully: 16/16 bootstrap steps (uv, Python 3.11, Git, Node.js, ripgrep/ffmpeg, repo clone, venv, Python deps, Node deps, Electron build, PATH, config templates, messaging SDKs, etc.)

**Problem**
On every launch, the desktop app reaches "Hermes backend is ready. Finalizing desktop startup" at 94%, then after ~45s shows:

  Hermes couldn't start
  The background gateway didn't come up.
  Timed out waiting for Hermes backend port announcement (45000ms)

This is 100% reproducible — it has happened on every single launch across multiple days (June 13–21, 2026) and after a full clean reinstall.

**Logs (from %LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\logs\desktop)**
Repeating cycle, port changes each time:
  [hermes] [boot] Resolving Hermes backend
  [hermes] [boot] Resolving Hermes runtime
  [hermes] [boot] Hermes runtime is ready
  [hermes] [boot] Starting Hermes backend via Hermes at ...\hermes-agent (venv: ...\hermes-agent\venv)
  [hermes] [boot] Waiting for Hermes backend to launch
  [hermes] HERMES_DASHBOARD_READY port=XXXXX
  [hermes] [boot] Waiting for Hermes backend to become ready
  [hermes] [boot] Hermes backend is ready. Finalizing desktop startup
  [hermes] Hermes backend exited (1073807364)
  ... (loop repeats with a new port)

Exit code 1073807364 = 0x40010004 = STATUS_DBG_TERMINATE_PROCESS — this looks like the process was forcibly terminated, not a normal crash.

**Logs (from %LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\logs\errors)**
At the exact moment the backend dies, every cycle:
  ConnectionResetError: [WinError 10054] An existing connection was forcibly closed by the remote host
  ...WARNING tui_gateway.ws: ws send failed peer=127.0.0.1:XXXXX
  ...event_type=WebSocketDisconnect error=
  ...ERROR asyncio: Exception in callback _ProactorBasePipeTransport._call_connection_lost(None)

**What I've already ruled out**
- File/venv locks from a previous crash-looping instance — fixed via full clean reinstall (confirmed: install now completes 16/16 every time)
- McAfee WebAdvisor — uninstalled, confirmed gone
- Windows Defender — Protection History is empty, no blocks logged
- Any other third-party antivirus/firewall/VPN — checked all ~99 installed applications, found none

**My hypothesis**
Your own Windows Native guide documents a known footgun: `os.kill(pid, 0)` on Windows maps to `CTRL_C_EVENT` and broadcasts Ctrl+C to the entire console process group (bpo-14484), which can kill sibling processes including the backend even when nothing is actually wrong. You mention this was migrated to `psutil.pid_exists()` / `gateway.status._pid_exists()` across 14 call sites in 11 files — but the symptom I'm seeing (forced termination immediately after the backend announces "ready", with a simultaneous loopback connection reset) matches this exact failure pattern. Is it possible a health-check or readiness-poll in the **desktop app's own Electron main process** (as opposed to the CLI/gateway code that was already migrated) still uses the old PID-check pattern on Windows?

**Request**
- Can you confirm whether the desktop app's "wait for backend ready" polling loop has been migrated off `os.kill(pid, 0)` on Windows?
- Any way to get a more verbose backend log right before the kill (e.g. an env var to log the Electron main process's process-management calls)?

Happy to provide the full desktop/errors log files if useful.

# feat(self-escalation): Dynamic thinking ON/OFF toggle via model self-detection

## Summary

Implements a dynamic thinking mode toggle where the model **self-detects** when a task requires deep reasoning, signals Hermes with a `[ESCALATE_THINKING: true]` marker, and Hermes automatically relaunches the iteration with thinking enabled.

**Production results: 5/5 tests passed (100%)**

---

## Test Results (Production)

### Qwen27B (port 8094 - RTX 3090) - Toggle réel thinking ON/OFF

| Test | Task Type | Time | Content | Reasoning | Marker | Expected | Result |
|------|-----------|------|---------|-----------|--------|----------|--------|
| 1 | Architecture analysis | 12.4s | 5336c | 0c | ✅ True | True | ✅ |
| 2 | Current time | 0.4s | 57c | 0c | ❌ False | False | ✅ |
| 3 | Code debugging | 9.9s | 4442c | 0c | ✅ True | True | ✅ |
| 4 | Text extraction | 0.5s | 80c | 0c | ❌ False | False | ✅ |
| 5 | Migration planning | 14.5s | 6867c | 0c | ✅ True | True | ✅ |

**Result: ✅ 5/5 CORRECT**

### Toggle réel thinking ON/OFF (Qwen27B)

| State | Time | Content | Reasoning | Ratio |
|-------|------|---------|-----------|-------|
| thinking OFF | 13.2s | 5374c | 0c | Baseline |
| thinking ON | 14.4s | 3116c | 3657c | 1.1x slower |

**Key insight:** thinking OFF is **instant** (0.4-0.5s) for simple tasks, **10-15s** for complex tasks (emits escalation marker).

### OpenRouter qwen3.7-max

| Task | Time | Marker | Result |
|------|------|--------|--------|
| Complex (proxy architecture) | 57.4s | ✅ True | ✅ |
| Simple (current time) | 17.1s | ❌ False | ✅ |

**Result: ✅ 2/2 tests passed**

---

## Implementation

### Files Changed

#### 1. `agent/self_escalation.py` (NEW — 175 lines)

Core module with all self-escalation logic:

```python
@dataclass
class ThinkingState:
    enabled: bool
    active: bool  # Current thinking state
    escalation_count: int
    max_escalations: int
    marker: str
    default_state: str

# Key functions
def load_thinking_config() -> ThinkingState
def inject_thinking_kwargs(api_kwargs, state, provider) -> dict
def detect_escalation(content, state) -> bool
def escalate(state) -> bool
def strip_escalation_marker(content, state) -> str
def inject_thinking_prompt(system_prompt, state) -> str
```

**Provider support:**
- `llama-cpp`, `custom` → top-level `chat_template_kwargs`
- `openrouter`, `nous` → `extra_body.chat_template_kwargs`

#### 2. `agent/conversation_loop.py` (MODIFIED — +50 lines)

**5 injection points:**

**A. Initialization (line ~537)**
```python
# Self-escalation: load config
try:
    from agent.self_escalation import load_thinking_config
    _thinking_state = load_thinking_config()
except Exception:
    _thinking_state = None
```

**B. Prompt injection (line ~775)**
```python
# Inject thinking instructions into system prompt
if _thinking_state and _thinking_state.enabled:
    from agent.self_escalation import inject_thinking_prompt
    effective_system = inject_thinking_prompt(effective_system, _thinking_state)
```

**C. API kwargs injection (line ~982)**
```python
# Inject chat_template_kwargs
if _thinking_state and _thinking_state.enabled:
    from agent.self_escalation import inject_thinking_kwargs
    api_kwargs = inject_thinking_kwargs(api_kwargs, _thinking_state, agent.provider)
```

**D. Escalation detection (line ~3718, before tool call check)**
```python
# Detect escalation request
if _thinking_state:
    from agent.self_escalation import detect_escalation, escalate, strip_escalation_marker
    if detect_escalation(assistant_message.content, _thinking_state):
        escalate(_thinking_state)
        assistant_message.content = strip_escalation_marker(assistant_message.content, _thinking_state)
        # Re-run iteration with thinking ON (no tool call)
        continue
```

**E. Reset on final response (line ~4073)**
```python
# Reset state for next user turn
if _thinking_state:
    _thinking_state.reset()
```

#### 3. `~/.hermes/config.yaml` (CONFIG)

New section added:
```yaml
thinking:
  enabled: true
  default_state: 'off'
  max_escalations_per_turn: 1
  detection_marker: '[ESCALATE_THINKING'
```

**Configuration options:**
| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `enabled` | bool | `true` | Enable/disable self-escalation |
| `default_state` | string | `'off'` | Initial thinking state (`'off'` or `'on'`) |
| `max_escalations_per_turn` | int | `1` | Max escalations per user turn (anti-loop) |
| `detection_marker` | string | `'[ESCALATE_THINKING'` | Marker to detect in model output |

---

## System Prompt

Optimized from v4 tests (8/8 = 100% success):

```
## SELF-ESCALATION (Dynamic Thinking Control)

Tu es en thinking OFF. Si la tâche est complexe (analyse approfondie, 
debug, planification, synthèse multi-sources), tu DOIS répondre avec 
ce format exact en premier :

[ESCALATE_THINKING: true]
[RAISON: pourquoi c'est complexe]

Puis tu peux donner une réponse préliminaire.

Si la tâche est simple (extraction, formatage, navigation, tool calls 
simples, réponses directes), réponds directement sans ce marqueur.

## MODE ACTUEL
thinking: {ON/OFF}
```

**Why this works:**
- Strict format `[ESCALATE_THINKING: true]` + `[RAISON: ...]` → unambiguous
- Clear examples: "analyse approfondie, debug" vs "extraction, formatage"
- State-awareness: model knows if currently ON or OFF
- Conservative default: OFF systematic, ON only on explicit request

---

## Anti-Loop Protection

**3 mechanisms prevent infinite escalation:**

1. **Counter limit**: `max_escalations_per_turn=1` (configurable)
2. **State check**: `if state.active: return False` (already ON → no escalation)
3. **Auto-reset**: State resets on each new user message

**Tested scenarios:**
- ✅ Complex task with escalation → thinking ON, no further escalation
- ✅ Simple task → no escalation
- ✅ Already ON → escalation blocked
- ✅ Max escalations reached → escalation blocked

---

## Performance Impact

### Token Savings
- **Simple tasks (60% of queries):** No reasoning tokens → ~40% faster
- **Complex tasks (30% of queries):** 1st call OFF (fast) + 2nd call ON (deep) → same quality, slightly slower
- **Edge cases (10%):** Model may not escalate when needed → graceful degradation

### Latency (Qwen27B)
- **Simple task:** 0.4-0.5s (instant)
- **Complex task:** 10-15s (emits escalation marker)
- **Complex task (relaunched ON):** 14.4s + 3657c reasoning

### Token Cost (estimated)
- Baseline (thinking ON always): 2500 reasoning tokens/turn
- Self-escalation (60% simple, 40% complex): ~1000 reasoning tokens/turn
- **Savings: ~60% reasoning tokens on average**

---

## Known Limitations

### 1. Prompt Cache Stability
**Issue:** Injection into `effective_system` changes the system prompt per iteration.
**Impact:** Breaks provider-side KV cache for cloud providers (OpenRouter, etc.)
**Mitigation:** Not an issue for local llama.cpp (no caching). For cloud providers, this trades cache efficiency for reasoning efficiency.

### 2. Fragile String Matching
**Issue:** Detection uses `state.marker in content` (simple substring match)
**Edge cases:**
- `[ESCALATE THINKING]` (no underscore) → not detected
- `[escalate_thinking]` (lowercase) → not detected
**Mitigation:** Could use regex `r"\[ESCALATE[_\-\s]*THINKING[:\s]+true\]"`

### 3. Reset Coverage
**Issue:** State only resets on final response (line 4073)
**Edge cases:** User interruption, budget exhaustion, API errors → state not reset
**Mitigation:** Could add `try/finally` around main loop or reset in loop exit handlers

### 4. Extra Body Merge Order
**Issue:** Provider profiles may override `extra_body` after injection
**Impact:** `chat_template_kwargs` could be lost
**Mitigation:** Verify merge order in `build_api_kwargs()` or inject after merge

### 5. No E2E Integration Tests
**Issue:** Only unit tests + manual API calls, no automated E2E
**Mitigation:** Could add test that mocks API responses and verifies escalation flow

---

## Code Diff Summary

```
agent/self_escalation.py                    | 175 ++++ (NEW)
agent/conversation_loop.py                  |  50 ++   (5 injection points)
~/.hermes/config.yaml                       |   5 +    (thinking section)
```

**Total:** 230 lines added (175 new module + 50 integration + 5 config)

---

## Installation

**1. Checkout branch:**
```bash
git checkout feat-self-escalation
```

**2. Add config to `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:**
```yaml
thinking:
  enabled: true
  default_state: 'off'
  max_escalations_per_turn: 1
  detection_marker: '[ESCALATE_THINKING'
```

**3. Restart gateway:**
```bash
hermes gateway restart
```

**4. Test:**
```bash
# Unit tests
cd ~/.hermes/hermes-agent
python3 -c "from agent.self_escalation import *; print('✅ Module loaded')"

# Integration test
python3 /tmp/test_qwen27b_suite.py  # Runs 5 production tests
```

---

## Future Improvements

1. **Regex-based detection** (more robust than substring match)
2. **Reset in `try/finally`** (cover all exit paths)
3. **E2E integration tests** (mock API + verify escalation flow)
4. **Metrics logging** (track escalation rate, token savings)
5. **Per-conversation toggle** (`/thinking on/off` command)

---

## References

- **Issue:** #50293
- **PR:** #50399
- **Branch:** `feat-self-escalation`
- **Commit:** `b57007adf`
- **Documentation:** `~/self-escalation-implementation-plan.md`
---

## Update — Prompt calibration (2026-06-22)

After initial deployment, we ran a **10-scenario test suite** against Qwen3.6-27B with the exact prompt injected by Hermes (`build_thinking_prompt()`):

### Before calibration (V1 prompt)

| Category | Score |
|----------|-------|
| Simple tasks → stay OFF | 66% (2/3) ❌ |
| Complex tasks → escalate | 66% (2/3) |
| Anti-loop (ON) | 100% (1/1) ✅ |
| **Overall** | **71% (5/7)** |

**Issues:** False positive on file listing (unnecessary escalation), false negative on basic debug (should have escalated).

### After calibration (V2 prompt with concrete examples)

| Category | Score |
|----------|-------|
| Simple tasks → stay OFF | 100% (5/5) ✅ |
| Complex tasks → escalate | 75% (3/4) |
| Anti-loop (ON) | 100% (1/1) ✅ |
| **Overall** | **90% (9/10)** |

**Changes to `build_thinking_prompt()`:**
- Added explicit "when to escalate" list (code analysis, traceback debug, contradictory data, multi-step planning)
- Added explicit "when NOT to escalate" list (math, translation, factual questions, file listing, simple tool calls)
- Added "borderline cases" section with clear rules

**Commit:** `0ce20511e` on branch `feat-skill-nudge-pruning`

### Remaining edge case

The only miss is a `ZeroDivisionError` debug — the model considers it too trivial for escalation. This is acceptable since it is genuinely a simple fix. The calibration trade-off favors precision (no false escalations on simple tasks) over recall.

---

## Update — Provider support fix (2026-06-22)

**All providers now use `extra_body`** (commit `bb1de6e2f`). The OpenAI SDK rejects unknown top-level kwargs, so even local llama.cpp servers need `chat_template_kwargs` nested in `extra_body`.

**Before:** `custom`/`llama-cpp` used top-level `chat_template_kwargs` (failed on auth-required endpoints)
**After:** All providers consistently use `api_kwargs.setdefault("extra_body", {})["chat_template_kwargs"] = {"enable_thinking": state.active}`

Verified with live API tests:

| State | Reasoning | Content | Time |
|-------|-----------|---------|------|
| OFF | 0 chars | 22 chars (direct answer) | 2.1s |
| ON | 364 chars | 0 chars (reasoning-only) | 0.9s |

items.body:
## Summary

Bedrock prompt caching works on current `main` (Claude routes through the AnthropicBedrock SDK / `anthropic_messages`, which injects `cache_control` and accounts cache tokens). But the **pricing layer can't price those cache tokens**, so `/usage` reports `Total cost: unknown` on every cached Bedrock session — the user can't see the savings caching produces.

Spun out of #11970 (closed: the caching itself is resolved on main by the 2026-05-12 dual-path routing). Originally surfaced by @JiaDe-Wu in the #11970 thread.

## Root cause

Two gaps in `agent/usage_pricing.py`:

1. **No cache cost fields on Bedrock pricing rows.** Every `("bedrock", "anthropic.claude-*")` `PricingEntry` carries only `input_cost_per_million` and `output_cost_per_million`. When a response has `cache_read_tokens` / `cache_write_tokens` but the entry has no `cache_read_cost_per_million` / `cache_write_cost_per_million`, `estimate_usage_cost()` returns `status="unknown"` (it bails with "cache-read pricing unavailable for route"). So any cached session prices as unknown.

2. **Cross-region inference-profile prefix not normalized.** Pricing keys are bare (`anthropic.claude-opus-4-7`), but the canonical Bedrock form for cross-region profiles is `us.anthropic.claude-opus-4-7` / `global.anthropic.claude-*` / `eu.anthropic.claude-*`. Those don't match the table. (`is_anthropic_bedrock_model()` already strips these prefixes for routing — the pricing path needs the same normalization.)

## Expected

`/usage` shows a real cost on Bedrock Claude sessions, including the cache-read discount, for both bare model ids and cross-region inference profiles.

## Fix sketch

- Add `cache_read_cost_per_million` (≈0.1× input) and `cache_write_cost_per_million` (≈1.25× input for 5m TTL, ≈2× for 1h) to the Bedrock Claude `PricingEntry` rows per the [Bedrock pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/).
- Normalize the cross-region prefix (`us.` / `global.` / `eu.` / `ap.` / `jp.`) in the Bedrock pricing lookup path, reusing the same prefix list as `is_anthropic_bedrock_model()`.

@JiaDe-Wu offered a `_normalize_bedrock_model_id` helper + cache pricing entries in the #11970 thread — that's a good starting point.

items.title: WhatsApp adapter doesn't support channel_prompts (system_hint)
items.body:
## Problem

The WhatsApp adapter (`gateway/platforms/whatsapp.py`) does not call `resolve_channel_prompt()` when building message events, so `whatsapp.channel_prompts` in `config.yaml` has no effect. Telegram and Slack both support this feature; WhatsApp is the only major adapter missing it.

This means WhatsApp sessions lose per-channel context guidance after the daily session reset — the agent has no ephemeral system_hint to re-orient itself, unlike Telegram where `channel_prompts` work correctly.

## Expected Behavior

`whatsapp.channel_prompts` in config.yaml should work the same as `telegram.channel_prompts`:

```yaml
whatsapp:
  channel_prompts:
    "1203xxx@g.us": |
      Family meal-planning group. 
```

The prompt should be injected as `channel_prompt` on each `MessageEvent`, so it is available as an ephemeral per-message hint regardless of session age.

## Actual Behavior

The WhatsApp adapter builds `MessageEvent` (in `_build_message_event`) without resolving `channel_prompt` from `self.config.extra`. The field is always `None`. Adding entries under `whatsapp.channel_prompts` in config.yaml is silently ignored.

## Root Cause

`resolve_channel_prompt()` in `gateway/platforms/base.py:1702` is only called from:
- `gateway/platforms/telegram.py:6728`
- `gateway/platforms/slack.py:2805`

`gateway/platforms/whatsapp.py` never calls it.

## Suggested Fix

In `_build_message_event()` (around line 1182), add channel_prompt resolution before constructing the `MessageEvent`, mirroring what the Telegram adapter does:

```python
# Per-channel ephemeral prompt (mirrors Telegram/Slack adapters).
from gateway.platforms.base import resolve_channel_prompt
_chat_id = data.get("chatId", "")
_channel_prompt = resolve_channel_prompt(self.config.extra, _chat_id)

return MessageEvent(
    text=body,
    message_type=msg_type,
    source=source,
    raw_message=data,
    message_id=data.get("messageId"),
    media_urls=cached_urls,
    media_types=media_types,
    channel_prompt=_channel_prompt,
)
```

The config bridging (`channel_prompts` → `config.extra`) is already handled generically in `gateway/config.py:986-991` and works for all platforms — no config-side changes needed.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.16.0 (2026.6.5)
- Confirmed still absent on origin/master (`3e354b61d`) as of 2026-06-22

## Context

I have applied this patch locally and verified it works end-to-end. Happy to open a PR if the maintainers want it.

items.body:
## Summary

A loopback-bound dashboard exposed through a trusted reverse proxy / Cloudflare Tunnel can load the HTTP UI successfully while the embedded Chat PTY WebSocket is rejected with `Session ended` / close code `1006`.

The affected setup has the dashboard bound to `127.0.0.1` and the proxy forwards HTTP/WS to it. The proxy preserves the browser `Origin` as the public dashboard URL but forwards `Host` to the loopback backend. HTTP passes the loopback Host guard, but WebSocket upgrades are rejected by `_ws_host_origin_reason()` because it requires the `Origin` netloc to match the loopback bound host.

## Observed behavior

Browser/UI:

- Chat page says: `Session ended.`
- Browser console: `[chat] PTY WebSocket closed code=1006`

Direct WebSocket repro before local fix:

```text
wss://dashboard.pojubot.org/api/pty?token=...&channel=...
Origin: https://dashboard.pojubot.org
=> HTTP 403
```

Local loopback WebSocket without public Origin worked, confirming the PTY endpoint itself was healthy.

## Expected behavior

When an operator explicitly configures a trusted public dashboard origin, WebSocket Origin validation should allow that exact origin while still rejecting unconfigured cross-site origins.

## Proposed fix

Honor an exact-origin allowlist from `HERMES_DASHBOARD_WS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` inside the WebSocket Host/Origin guard. The patch intentionally **does not support wildcards** because this hook bypasses the normal same-host check and broad shared-domain patterns could weaken the DNS-rebinding guard.

Verification performed locally:

```text
python -m py_compile hermes_cli/web_server.py tests/hermes_cli/test_dashboard_auth_ws_auth.py
python -m pytest tests/hermes_cli/test_dashboard_auth_ws_auth.py -q -o 'addopts='
# 48 passed, 1 existing xdist mark warning
```

Independent review result: passed; no security concerns or logic errors after changing the allowlist to exact-origin only.

## Patch

```diff
From 40cbf67153313f773e26bf53fc6e9a2cabebee3d Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: root <root@srv1699754.hstgr.cloud>
Date: Sun, 21 Jun 2026 22:33:19 +0300
Subject: [PATCH] fix(dashboard): honor explicit websocket origins

---
 hermes_cli/web_server.py                      | 35 ++++++++++++++++
 .../hermes_cli/test_dashboard_auth_ws_auth.py | 42 +++++++++++++++++++
 2 files changed, 77 insertions(+)

diff --git a/hermes_cli/web_server.py b/hermes_cli/web_server.py
index 74ea81825..f295864f7 100644
--- a/hermes_cli/web_server.py
+++ b/hermes_cli/web_server.py
@@ -10967,6 +10967,39 @@ _VALID_CHANNEL_RE = re.compile(r"^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,128}$")
 # Starlette's TestClient reports the peer as "testclient"; treat it as
 # loopback so tests don't need to rewrite request scope.
 _LOOPBACK_HOSTS = frozenset({"127.0.0.1", "::1", "localhost", "testclient"})
+_WS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS_ENV = "HERMES_DASHBOARD_WS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS"
+
+
+def _origin_matches_pattern(origin: str, pattern: str) -> bool:
+    """Return True when a browser Origin matches an explicit allowlist entry.
+
+    Entries must be full exact origins (``https://dashboard.example.org``).
+    Wildcards are intentionally unsupported here: this hook bypasses the normal
+    same-host Origin check for loopback dashboards behind a trusted proxy, so a
+    broad shared-domain pattern would weaken the DNS-rebinding guard.
+    """
+    parsed_origin = urllib.parse.urlparse(origin.rstrip("/"))
+    parsed_pattern = urllib.parse.urlparse(pattern.strip().rstrip("/"))
+    if parsed_origin.scheme not in {"http", "https"}:
+        return False
+    if parsed_pattern.scheme not in {"http", "https"}:
+        return False
+    if parsed_origin.scheme.lower() != parsed_pattern.scheme.lower():
+        return False
+
+    origin_netloc = parsed_origin.netloc.lower()
+    pattern_netloc = parsed_pattern.netloc.lower()
+    if not origin_netloc or not pattern_netloc or "*" in pattern_netloc:
+        return False
+    return origin_netloc == pattern_netloc
+
+
```

items.body:
## Summary
When one stdio MCP server fails to spawn (e.g. its wrapper exits non-zero / `exec: not found`), it is restarted in a tight loop, and that restart storm **destabilizes the entire MCP subsystem** — *other, healthy* MCP servers' tools begin returning `{"error":"Unknown tool: X"}` to agent workers, even though those tools remain **declared** in the model's function list.

## Environment
- hermes-agent 0.17.0 (Docker, Linux)

## What happened
A `perseus` MCP wrapper ran a bare `exec perseus mcp serve`, but the **gateway spawns MCP servers with a minimal PATH** that excluded the binary dir → `exec: perseus: not found` on every spawn. `logs/mcp-stderr.log` showed ~10+ restart cycles in 8 minutes. The co-located `mimir` MCP server logged `ready` on each cycle, yet its `mimir_*` tools were **also** "Unknown tool" for agent workers. Fixing only the perseus wrapper (absolute path) restored **both** servers' tools.

## Two distinct problems
1. **No isolation / no backoff** — one failing MCP server should not take down others. Each stdio server should be supervised independently with exponential backoff + a circuit breaker, not a shared tight restart loop.
2. **Misleading failure mode** — while a server is disconnected, its tools should either not be advertised to the model, or the dispatch error should be `MCP server 'X' unavailable` rather than `Unknown tool: X` (which implies the tool doesn't exist and sends agents down the wrong debugging path).

## Repro sketch
Register two stdio MCP servers; make one's command fail to exec (e.g. a wrapper relying on `$PATH` for a binary not on the gateway's PATH). Observe the other server's tools intermittently return "Unknown tool" for agent tasks while `hermes mcp test <healthy-server>` still passes.

items.title: feat(desktop/windows): show update progress before the desktop exits so it doesn't look like a crash
items.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #50238 (fixed in #50381). The backend restart-loop is now closed by the update-in-progress marker + launch gate, but the *trigger* that lures users into relaunching mid-update remains: **on the Windows in-app update path the desktop window vanishes with no progress feedback, which looks like a crash.**

## Where

`apps/desktop/electron/main.cjs` `applyUpdates()` (Windows hand-off path): after `releaseBackendLockForUpdate`, it spawns the detached `hermes-setup.exe --update`, logs `exiting desktop to release venv shim`, then `app.quit()`s 600ms later:

```js
rememberLog(`[updates] launched updater: ...; exiting desktop to release venv shim`)
setTimeout(() => { app.quit() }, 600)
```

The Tauri updater spawns its own progress window, but there's a visible gap between our `app.quit()` and the updater window appearing. During that gap the user sees nothing — the app they clicked "Update" in just disappeared. The natural reaction is to relaunch, which is exactly the scenario #50381 now has to defend against (park-until-done).

## Why it's worth doing

The #50381 marker/gate makes the relaunch *safe* (no more loop), but a user who relaunches still hits an "Update in progress…" wait instead of a smooth experience. Closing the feedback gap removes the incentive to relaunch in the first place.

## Possible directions (not prescriptive)

- Show a brief, explicit "Updating Hermes — this window will close and reopen automatically. Please don't relaunch." overlay/toast *before* the 600ms `app.quit()`, with enough dwell that the user reads it.
- Or keep a minimal always-on-top splash alive across the hand-off so there's never a blank-screen moment.
- Verify the Tauri updater window is actually foregrounded on Windows (DETACHED_PROCESS + windowsHide handling) so it surfaces promptly.

## Scope / non-goals

- Pure UX; does **not** touch the marker/gate mutual-exclusion logic from #50381 (that stays as the safety net).
- Windows in-app update path is the priority (where the loop originated); macOS/Linux feedback can be folded in if cheap.

## Related

- #50238 — the restart-loop bug (root cause)
- #50381 — the merged fix (marker + launch gate)
- #49606 — detect failed in-app update and guide user to terminal fallback

items.title: session.usage.context_used can fall back to cumulative session_total_tokens for external context engines
items.body:
## Summary

When an external context engine is active, the host `session.usage` path can report impossible context usage values because `context_used` falls back to cumulative `session_total_tokens` instead of current prompt/context occupancy.

This is currently tracked from the hermes-lcm side as stephenschoettler/hermes-lcm#251, but there is not yet a narrow Hermes Agent upstream issue for the host-side contract.

## Concrete external-engine case

With `context.engine: lcm`, operators observed status-bar values such as:

```text
304k / 120k
1.9m / 120k
4.2m / 120k
```

while the real active prompt/context was roughly 55k to 60k tokens and no multi-million-token prompt existed.

The LCM-side evidence indicates the TUI is not inventing the value on its own. It renders `session.usage.context_used`, and the host usage path is where the bad fallback happens.

## Suspected host-side root cause

In `tui_gateway/server.py`, the current shape is:

```python
ctx_used = getattr(comp, "last_prompt_tokens", 0) or usage["total"] or 0
usage["context_used"] = ctx_used
```

If the active context engine does not provide a truthy `last_prompt_tokens` value in that path, Hermes falls back to `usage["total"]`, which is cumulative `session_total_tokens`.

That makes the status bar show lifetime session accumulation instead of current context occupancy.

## Why this is a bug

`context_used` is a current-window/runtime occupancy signal.

`session_total_tokens` is cumulative lifetime session usage.

Those are not interchangeable. Falling back from the former to the latter produces impossible values and misleading 100% clamp behavior for external context engines even when the active prompt remains well within the model context window.

## Expected behavior

When an external context engine is active, Hermes should expose a current context-occupancy value that reflects the active prompt/runtime window, not cumulative session usage.

If the host cannot derive a trustworthy current occupancy value, it should prefer an explicit unknown/absent state over silently substituting cumulative totals.

## Acceptance criteria

- `session.usage.context_used` does not silently fall back to cumulative `session_total_tokens` for external context engines.
- The TUI/gateway status bar shows a current-window value or a clearly-unknown value, but not a cumulative lifetime total in the `context_used` slot.
- The fix works for external context engines such as `context.engine: lcm` without regressing built-in compressor behavior.

## Related

- stephenschoettler/hermes-lcm#251
- Related but not exact neighboring issues in Hermes Agent: #23798, #18260, #35823

items.title: manual gateway /compress temporary agent drops platform metadata and can duplicate external-engine transcript rows
items.body:
## Summary

Manual gateway `/compress` can construct a temporary host agent without preserving the original platform metadata and stable gateway session key. For external context engines that bind ingest/source attribution to the host agent metadata, that can cause the retained transcript tail to be ingested under the wrong source and later duplicated when the normal platform-bound session resumes.

This is currently tracked from the hermes-lcm side as stephenschoettler/hermes-lcm#253, but there is not yet a narrow Hermes Agent upstream issue for the host-side gateway contract.

## Concrete external-engine case

For `context.engine: lcm`, live evidence showed the same retained Telegram transcript tail first ingested as `source=cli` during manual `/compress`, then later ingested again as `source=telegram` after normal session replay/restart.

Observed duplicate source pair:

```text
cli,telegram
```

The core user-visible invariant that breaks is:

```text
manual Telegram /compress should not store the retained Telegram tail once as cli and later again as telegram
```

## Suspected host-side root cause

`gateway/run.py::_handle_compress_command` creates a temporary `AIAgent(...)` for manual compression using the active `session_id`, but without preserving the same gateway metadata that normal gateway turns use:

- missing `platform=...`
- missing stable `gateway_session_key=...`

That means an external context engine can see the temporary agent as an unbound/default host session rather than the original platform-bound conversation.

## Why this is a bug

Manual `/compress` is host-side maintenance on an existing gateway conversation. It should preserve the same session/platform identity contract as normal gateway turns.

If the temporary agent loses that metadata, any external context engine or platform-aware ingest path can misattribute the retained tail and create duplicate raw rows or mixed-source lineage for the same conversation.

## Expected behavior

Manual gateway `/compress` should construct any temporary agent with the same platform and stable gateway session identity as the live platform session being compressed.

For example, the temporary agent should preserve the metadata needed so external context engines bind the operation to the original platform conversation instead of falling back to an unbound/default host source.

## Acceptance criteria

- Manual gateway `/compress` preserves the original platform metadata and stable gateway session key when constructing its temporary agent.
- Running manual `/compress` on a platform-bound session does not cause the retained tail to be ingested under a different host source classification.
- External context engines can treat manual `/compress` as maintenance on the same conversation, not as a new anonymous/default host session.

## Related

- stephenschoettler/hermes-lcm#253
- Related but not exact neighboring issues in Hermes Agent: #45132, #41858, #42814, #48911, #45157
